newsitem.title: CHINA: China foreign currency share pessimism prevails.
newsitem.headline: China foreign currency share pessimism prevails.

text.p: China's foreign currency B share markets, stuck in a deep depression for two years despite a bull run on the domestic markets, will remain in the doldrums for the rest of 1996, stock analysts said on Friday.

They cited the lack of government support, including repeated bans on local Chinese trading in B shares, and declining overseas investor confidence due to poor company results as the two most important factors.

By Friday's close, Shanghai's B share index was little changed at 48.239 points against 47.69 points at the close of the last trading day in 1995. Shanghai's A share index surged about 90 percent over the same period.
During this period, Shenzhen's B share index rose about 50 percent to 90.00 points, compared to a rise of more than 200 percent on the exchange's A share market.
Trading volume on the B share markets is only a fraction of that on the A share markets.
Combined average daily turnover of the A markets is about 20 billion yuan ($2.41 billion) against only tens of millions of dollars on the two B share markets.
"The (B share) markets have become extremely dull," said one broker with a major Chinese brokerage. "There is no hope that they will recover before the end of this year."
A stock analyst said repeated bans on local Chinese trading B shares showed that the central government would not allow the markets to expand quickly in the short term.
"The authorities seem to have no clear model for the B share markets in their minds," the analyst said.
In contrast, policy support for the A share markets, including morale-boosting speeches by top securities officials, was a key factor for the markets' rise this year, analysts said.

Analysts said B share companies as a whole had performed worse than A share firms in the past two years, mainly due to poor management and being hit harder by Beijing's austerity measures in force since 1993.
"Foreign investor confidence has greatly been hurt by the past two years of poor results by B share firms," said a Shanghai-based investment analyst with a Western brokerage.
"Unless there is solid evidence that their performance will improve in the short term, the B markets will not recover."
Analysts said recent surges of stocks on the Hong Kong exchange, including shares of Chinese firms, were another major negative factor for the B share markets.

"Foreigners are shifting investments to H-share companies," said an analyst with a Shanghai branch of a Hong Kong brokerage. "H share prices are rising and the performance of the companies is better (than that of B share companies)."
Beijing established the B share markets in 1992 to allow major companies to raise foreign funds. Chinese securities rules say that only foreigners may buy the B shares.

In the first two years, B shares were almost solely in the hands of foreigners but a deep market depression since mid-1994 persuaded the two exchanges to quietly allow local investors to trade B shares.
By June and July this year, local participation peaked, with brokers estimating that Chinese accounted for 60 percent of B share trading in Shenzhen and 40 percent in Shanghai.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission, the watchdog, then issued a series of orders re-affirming the ban on local trading in B shares. Brokers say this sharply reduced the scale of local participation and B share trading volume.
